name: Ruffin v. Davis
court: Fourth Circuit (from the District of South Carolina)
topic: Fourth Amendment deadly force against a fleeing armed teenager who made no threatening movement with his gun; qualified immunity denied; Barnes v. Felix applied
summary: A Columbia, South Carolina officer chased a high school senior who ran from him during a COVID curfew, saw that the teenager had a gun, and fired ten rounds as the teenager stood up from a crouch and ran, killing him. The Fourth Circuit affirmed the denial of qualified immunity. Accepting the district court's view of the disputed facts, the teenager was armed and had ignored commands but made no furtive or threatening movement with the weapon, and it was clearly established in the Fourth Circuit since 2013 that an officer may not use deadly force against an armed suspect unless the officer or another person is threatened with the weapon. The court applied Barnes v. Felix to say the moment the teenager crouched was not the one that mattered most once he turned away and ran. It is taught for the rule that being armed and disobedient is not by itself a justification for deadly force.
coverage: The full published opinion by Chief Judge Diaz, joined by Judges Thacker and Berner, including all footnotes, was read from https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCOURTS-ca4-25-01318/pdf/USCOURTS-ca4-25-01318-0.pdf. The slip opinion is headed USCA4 Appeal: 25-1318, Doc. 46, filed April 29, 2026, Published, appeal from the District of South Carolina at Columbia (3:23-cv-01425-SAL), argued January 28, 2026, decided April 29, 2026.
No reporter citation was available in the sources read. The brief cites the docket and decision date.

The Fourth Circuit cases the court relied on (Cooper v. Sheehan, Knibbs v. Momphard, Aleman v. City of Charlotte, Hensley v. Price, Benton v. Layton) were not read; they are described as the Ruffin court described them. Barnes v. Felix was read for a companion brief.

The opinion arose on an interlocutory appeal from the denial of summary judgment on qualified immunity. The court accepted the district court's identification of the undisputed facts and its finding that the teenager's movements were otherwise disputed, and said it lacked jurisdiction to revisit those factual determinations. The body camera and surveillance videos were not viewed for this brief.
No petition for rehearing or certiorari was checked. The opinion is recent and its subsequent history is unknown to this brief.

Citation as written in the brief: No. 25-1318 (4th Cir. Apr. 29, 2026). The source read gave it as: No. 25-1318 (4th Cir. Apr. 29, 2026) (published; reporter citation not yet available in the sources read).
facts:
The facts are as the Fourth Circuit recounted them in the light most favorable to the plaintiff. In April 2020, South Carolina was under a COVID 19 stay at home and curfew order. One evening, City of Columbia police officer Kevin Davis responded to a report of teenagers riding bikes and looking into cars in a residential area. He saw J.R., a high school senior, walking alone on the sidewalk with no bike in sight. Davis later said he saw J.R. step behind a house and reappear with a bag; the plaintiff said J.R. had the bag, a gift from his mother, the whole time. When Davis approached, J.R. ran, and Davis chased him.

Body camera footage captured the chase, which lasted about 42 seconds; a high school parking lot camera captured parts of it. Davis shouted three times for J.R. to stop running; J.R. did not. About 23 seconds in, J.R. stopped briefly and crouched near the fence of an empty parking lot. The parties dispute whether he crouched deliberately or tripped. Davis claimed he then saw J.R. reach to the bottom of his pant leg to retrieve a gun; the court did not accept that allegation as true, though it was undisputed that J.R. had a gun. Davis closed the distance, yelled several times for J.R. to get on the ground, drew his firearm, and shouted for J.R. to show his hands. J.R. did not comply; he stood up and started running. Davis fired and missed. As J.R. kept running, Davis fired nine more rounds, hitting him in the forehead and killing him. Davis incorrectly told investigators he had fired approximately four shots.

During the investigation Davis said J.R. turned his head toward him during the chase in what Davis believed was an attempt to turn his body and raise the firearm toward him, and said he heard a gunshot. Police recovered a gun next to J.R.'s hand. Forensic evidence showed J.R. had been carrying the gun but had not fired it.

J.R.'s mother sued Davis under 42 U.S.C. section 1983 for, among other things, excessive force. Davis moved for summary judgment on qualified immunity. A magistrate judge found it difficult to discern J.R.'s movements from either video, considered that he could have tripped while fleeing in fear and that the gun could have fallen, and noted that he never pointed the gun at Davis and never fired. The district court adopted the recommendation. It found three undisputed facts: J.R. possessed a firearm; J.R. ignored Davis's repeated commands to stop running, get on the ground, and show his hands; and J.R. turned to face Davis in the final moments of the chase, as shown by the location of the fatal wound. It found no undisputed evidence that J.R. made a furtive or threatening movement with his weapon and denied qualified immunity. Davis appealed.
holding:
Affirmed. Chief Judge Diaz wrote for a unanimous panel.

Jurisdiction. On an interlocutory appeal the court cannot review the district court's determination that genuine disputes of fact exist, but it can decide whether, accepting the facts as the district court viewed them, the officer violated clearly established law. The court therefore asked whether the three undisputed facts entitled Davis to qualified immunity.

The constitutional violation. Deadly force is a seizure that the Fourth Amendment permits only when the officer has probable cause to believe the suspect poses a threat of serious physical harm to the officer or others (Garner), judged by the totality of the circumstances under the Graham factors. The severity of the crime favored J.R.: an investigation of teenagers looking into cars does not suggest a crime, let alone a serious one. The evasion factor favored Davis: J.R. undisputedly ignored commands to stop, show his hands, and get on the ground. The decisive factor was the immediate threat. Davis argued he reasonably perceived danger because J.R. ignored commands, visibly held a handgun, crouched, and turned his head toward him. The court was not persuaded. The district court found the evidence of J.R.'s movements at the crouch ambiguous, and the court of appeals lacked jurisdiction to revisit that. In any event, citing Barnes v. Felix, the court said the moment J.R. was crouched was not the one that matters most, because any justification Davis might have had when J.R. crouched dissipated when J.R. turned away and ran. The court said it had not put on chronological blinders: even considering that J.R. crouched briefly, ignored commands, and was armed, a jury could find Davis acted unreasonably. Deadly force cannot be used simply because a suspect is armed and has ignored commands (Aleman). An officer need not wait until a gun is pointed at him (Knibbs), but the officer or another person must be threatened with the weapon (Cooper v. Sheehan), and a weapon justifies deadly force only if the person makes some furtive or other threatening movement with it. Whether J.R. made any such movement at any point was disputed. The only undisputed movement was turning his head to face Davis in the final moments, and viewed in the plaintiff's favor that was not a movement that could reasonably be perceived as dangerous. The court acknowledged split second judgments and the prohibition on hindsight but concluded that a reasonable officer would have recognized he faced no imminent threat when an armed suspect was running away and made no threatening movement with his weapon. Davis's use of deadly force therefore violated J.R.'s Fourth Amendment rights on the facts as viewed by the district court.

Clearly established. The question was whether it was clearly established in April 2020 that an officer violates the Fourth Amendment by using deadly force against an armed suspect who runs, ignores commands, crouches momentarily before running again, turns his head to look behind him while running, but does not raise his weapon or make any other threatening movement. No case had identical facts, but that does not preclude a finding that the right was clearly established. Since Cooper v. Sheehan in 2013 the Fourth Circuit has repeatedly warned officers that it is not objectively reasonable to use deadly force against an armed suspect unless, based on a reasonable assessment, the officer or another person is threatened with the weapon, and Knibbs confirmed that failure to obey commands by a person with a weapon justifies deadly force only if the person makes a furtive or other threatening movement with it, citing several pre 2020 cases. Because there was no undisputed evidence that J.R. threatened Davis with his weapon or otherwise, Davis violated J.R.'s clearly established right to be free from deadly force when posing no threat.
notDecided:
Whether Davis in fact used excessive force. The court held that a jury could so find on the facts as the district court viewed them; the disputed facts about J.R.'s movements at the crouch remain for trial.

Whether J.R. reached for his gun at the crouch. Davis said he saw J.R. retrieve a gun from his pant leg; the court did not accept that as true, and the district court found the video ambiguous. If a jury accepts Davis's account, the analysis of the shots fired as J.R. rose could differ.

Whether the initial pursuit or the decision to draw was reasonable. The case concerned the shooting.

Whether the officer's statements to investigators about the number of shots and the gunshot he said he heard affect credibility. The court noted both discrepancies in footnotes without ruling on them.

Claims against the city, the police department, and the chief, which the plaintiff dismissed by stipulation.
inPractice:
Ruffin states a rule that officers in every circuit should understand even though it is Fourth Circuit law: being armed and refusing commands is not, by itself, a justification for deadly force. The person must be threatening someone with the weapon, which the Fourth Circuit describes as a furtive or threatening movement with it. The court was careful to say an officer need not wait until the gun is pointed at him. But a suspect who is running away with a gun he has not raised, and whose only undisputed movement is turning his head, is not an immediate threat on the plaintiff's version of events.

The case also shows how Barnes v. Felix works for both sides. The officer argued the crouch was the moment of danger. The court said the crouch was not the moment that mattered most, because whatever justification existed then dissipated when the teenager turned away and ran, and the shots were fired as he ran. The court expressly said it had not put on chronological blinders: it considered the crouch, the commands, and the weapon, and still found a jury question. Barnes requires courts to look at everything; it does not freeze the justification at its highest point.

Compare Handy v. Jones, decided by the Ninth Circuit five months later. There the armed man was suspected of a violent assault, had been reported waiting for police with a shotgun, refused commands, and advanced on officers waving the weapon and cursing; the court held he was an immediate threat regardless of where the gun was pointed. In Ruffin the suspected offense was looking into cars, the person was a teenager running away, and the gun was never raised. The two cases together mark the line: direction of travel, the nature of the suspected crime, and what the person is doing with the weapon decide whether an armed, noncompliant person is an immediate threat.

Dr. Sowards teaches Ruffin in the deadly force line as a flight case under Garner. The training lesson is that flight by an armed person who is not threatening anyone is a containment and pursuit problem, not a deadly force justification.
trainIt:
Teach the distinction between armed and threatening. Put the Fourth Circuit's formulation on the board: a weapon justifies deadly force only if the person makes some furtive or other threatening movement with it, and the officer need not wait until it is pointed at him. Have students describe, in specific physical terms, what a threatening movement with a handgun looks like during a foot pursuit (the gun coming up, the body turning with the weapon oriented toward the officer, the hand moving the gun from carry to presentation) and what does not (running away, a glance over the shoulder, holding the gun at the side).

Teach the foot pursuit decision. The chase lasted 42 seconds over a report of teenagers looking into cars during a curfew. Ask students what the objective of the pursuit was, what the risk was to the officer and to the community if the teenager escaped, and what containment and backup options existed. The court weighed the minor nature of the suspected offense heavily. Students should learn that the severity of the crime factor is part of the deadly force calculus, not just the arrest calculus.

Teach the sequence under Barnes. Build the timeline: commands to stop, the crouch, commands to get on the ground and show hands, the gun seen, the teenager stands and runs, the first shot, nine more shots as he runs. Have students identify the moment of greatest perceived danger and then explain why the court said that moment was not the one that mattered most once the person turned away. The lesson is that the justification must exist when each shot is fired, and that a court will look at the whole sequence.

Teach accuracy in statements. The officer told investigators he fired approximately four shots when he fired ten, and said he heard a gunshot when the forensic evidence showed the teenager never fired. The court noted both in footnotes. Train students that statements after a shooting should be made with care and that physical evidence will be compared to them.

Teach the contrast with Handy for the full picture of an armed, noncompliant subject.
caution: Read in full from govinfo. The opinion is published and binding in the Fourth Circuit; it is not binding in the Ninth Circuit, though its reasoning applies Garner and Barnes v. Felix. No reporter citation was available, and subsequent history is unknown. The decision is an interlocutory ruling affirming the denial of summary judgment; the facts are the plaintiff's version as the district court viewed them, key facts about the teenager's movements are disputed, and no court has found that the officer used excessive force. The videos were not viewed for this brief.

applications.title: Armed and disobedient is not enough
applications.body: Deadly force cannot be used simply because a suspect is armed and has ignored commands. The officer or another person must be threatened with the weapon, shown by a furtive or other threatening movement with it. A gun carried by a person running away, never raised, did not meet that test on the plaintiff's version.

applications.title: No need to wait for the muzzle, but need a threat
applications.body: The Fourth Circuit repeated that an officer need not wait until a gun is pointed at him. The dividing line is a movement with the weapon that signals intent to use it, not mere possession.

applications.title: The justification must exist when the shots are fired
applications.body: Applying Barnes, the court said the crouch was not the moment that mattered most because any justification then dissipated when the teenager turned away and ran, and all ten shots were fired as he ran.

applications.title: Severity of the crime counts in deadly force
applications.body: The report was teenagers looking into cars during a curfew. The court said that investigation did not suggest a crime, let alone a serious one, and weighed that factor for the teenager.

applications.title: Statements will be checked against evidence
applications.body: The officer told investigators he fired about four shots and heard a gunshot; he fired ten and the teenager never fired. Post incident statements should be made carefully and will be compared with the physical evidence.

quiz.q: What rule did the Fourth Circuit apply to decide whether deadly force against the armed, fleeing teenager was reasonable?
options: Any armed suspect who ignores commands may be shot

Deadly force may be used against an armed suspect only if, based on a reasonable assessment, the officer or another person is threatened with the weapon, shown by a furtive or other threatening movement with it
Deadly force may never be used against a fleeing suspect
Deadly force requires a warning shot
quiz.teach: The court relied on Cooper v. Sheehan, Knibbs, and Aleman. It said an officer need not wait until a gun is pointed at him but that possession plus disobedience is not enough.

quiz.q: How did the court use Barnes v. Felix in Ruffin?
options: To hold that only the crouch mattered
To hold that the crouch was not the moment that mattered most because any justification dissipated when the teenager turned away and ran, while still considering the whole sequence
To exclude the body camera video
quiz.teach: The court said it had not put on chronological blinders; it considered the crouch, the commands, and the weapon, and still concluded a jury could find the shots fired at a fleeing suspect unreasonable.

quiz.q: Since when did the Fourth Circuit say the relevant right was clearly established?
options: Since Garner in 1985 only as a general matter

Since Cooper v. Sheehan in 2013, with Knibbs confirming that failure to obey commands by an armed person justifies deadly force only if the person makes a furtive or threatening movement with the weapon
quiz.teach: The court said it had repeatedly warned officers since 2013 that deadly force against an armed suspect is unreasonable unless the officer or another person is threatened with the weapon, so the right was clearly established in April 2020.
